title: India's Diabetes Surge Threatens the Eyesight of Millions, Experts Warn
excerpt: With over 101 million Indians living with diabetes and 85% never screened for eye damage, the country's new 2025 guidelines push AI-assisted retinal screening — a warning that applies to South Asian communities abroad as well.
body:
• More than 101 million Indians have diabetes, and an estimated 12.5% of them — over 12 million people — have diabetic retinopathy, with 4% living with the vision-threatening form.
  • Around 85% of Indian diabetics have never had a retinal examination, leaving millions undiagnosed until vision damage is irreversible.
  • India's revised 2025 National Guidelines for diabetic retinopathy management push AI-assisted screening and aim for 80% screening coverage among diabetics, with a simple call to action: get your eyes checked yearly.
  • If you have diabetes, doctors recommend a dilated eye exam at diagnosis and at least once a year after — diabetic retinopathy is silent in its early stages and treatable only if caught early. This applies whether you live in India, the US, or the UK.

India's diabetes epidemic is producing a second crisis, one that is quietly taking people's sight. With more than 101 million Indians living with diabetes, the country's eye-care system is now confronting a surge of diabetic retinopathy — a complication that damages the blood vessels of the retina and is already one of India's leading causes of preventable blindness.

Recent population research puts the scale in stark terms. The SMART India study, a multicentre screening project across 10 states and one union territory covering 42,146 people aged 40 and above, found a nationally weighted prevalence of 12.5% for diabetic retinopathy and 4.0% for vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy among people with diabetes, according to findings published in The Lancet Global Health. Applied to India's diabetic population, that means roughly 12 million people have some form of the disease and about 3 to 4 million face an immediate threat to their vision.

A burden decades in the making

India's diabetes numbers have climbed relentlessly for four decades, and the ICMR-INDIAB study — India's largest diabetes survey, conducted with the Union Health Ministry — now estimates over 101 million diabetics nationwide, with hundreds of millions more living with prediabetes. Diabetes damages small blood vessels throughout the body, and the retina's delicate capillaries are among the first casualties. High blood sugar weakens vessel walls, causing them to leak, swell shut, or sprout fragile new vessels that bleed into the eye — the mechanism behind diabetic retinopathy.

The cruel part is the silence. The disease is typically asymptomatic in its early stages, when laser treatment or anti-VEGF injections can still halt it. Untreated vision-threatening disease progresses fast: research cited in Scientific Reports finds that 26% of people with untreated vision-threatening retinopathy develop severe vision impairment within two years. By the time blurred vision or floaters prompt a visit to an eye doctor, the damage is often permanent.

Compounding the problem, blood sugar control in India is poor. The SMART India study found glycemic control was suboptimal in about 75% of participants with known diabetes — a finding researchers describe as a warning that an epidemic of diabetes complications is underway.

The screening gap — and the 2025 response

The deeper failure is detection. An estimated 85% of Indian diabetic patients are unaware that diabetes can affect vision and have never undergone a retinal examination, according to the Vision 2020 India programme. Many physicians who manage diabetes — diabetologists, endocrinologists, and primary-care doctors — do not consistently refer patients for retinal screening, so the disease is found only when it has already done its worst.

India has now responded with its first updated national framework in a decade. Vision 2020: The Right to Sight – India released the revised National Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Retinopathy in 2025, replacing the 2015 manual. The guidelines call for AI-assisted, digitally integrated screening using CDSCO-cleared applications, non-mydriatic and smartphone-based fundus cameras for grading, and the training of non-ophthalmologist personnel — optometrists, nurses, paramedics, and Ayush staff — to conduct screening at primary-care and community level. The stated ambition: 80% diabetic retinopathy screening coverage among India's diabetic population.

"By prioritizing timely and systematic screening, we can identify disease much earlier — significantly improving outcomes. Evidence shows that early intervention can halve the risk of severe vision loss."

— Dr Vishali Gupta, President, Vitreo Retinal Society of India

The guidelines' public message is deliberately simple: "Check yearly and See Clearly."

The diaspora is not exempt

This story travels well beyond India. Asian Indians carry what researchers call a distinct phenotype — high intra-abdominal fat and insulin resistance at comparatively low body weight — that predisposes them to early-onset diabetes, according to a review published in the journal Cureus. South Asian communities in the United States and United Kingdom develop type 2 diabetes at higher rates and younger ages than the general population, and at lower BMI thresholds than standard screening cutoffs reflect.

The consequence is that the screening logic applies everywhere. A dilated eye exam at diabetes diagnosis, repeated yearly, is the standard doctors recommend for catching retinopathy while it is still treatable — and the disease respects no borders. For Indian-American and British-Indian families, where diabetes often runs through the household, the annual eye check belongs on the same calendar as blood work.

What to watch

The 2025 guidelines are a framework, not a finished system. Their success will depend on whether AI-assisted screening actually reaches primary health centres and whether referral networks connect screen-detected patients to retina specialists for treatment. Watch for the first state-level coverage numbers under the new framework — the gap between the 80% target and today's near-zero screening baseline is where the policy will be judged. Also watch the technology story: validated AI grading tools could make mass screening economically feasible for the first time, not just in India but in other low-resource settings facing the same diabetes-driven wave of vision loss.
